# R3 Commentary 4–6:9 — Extraction Digest

Source slice: `R3_comm_4_6_2098_2562.txt` (raw lines 2098–2562).
Commentator: Tremper Longman III, NICOT Ecclesiastes.
Scope: Qohelet’s quest continues — Eccl 4:1 through 6:9 (includes temple caution 4:17–5:6 ET 5:1–7; wealth unit 5:10–6:9 ET; SUMMARY of 4:17–6:9). Stops before D. Qohelet’s Wise Advice (6:10).
Note: Lines L2098–L2101 are residual chapter-3 summary (bridge into 4); claims below start from §3 “Better Off Dead (4:1–3).”

---

### C-R3-01
**Locus:** L2103–L2106; 4:1–3 section intro
**Quote/anchor:** “The opening section of chapter 4 raises the issue of oppression in the world, particularly the exploitation of the powerless by the powerful. Qohelet’s observation on oppression leads to his, by this time not surprising, conclusion that, though we may lament the existence of oppression, we cannot do anything about it.”
**Claim:** Longman frames 4:1–3 as Qohelet’s observation of oppression (powerful exploiting powerless) that ends in resigned helplessness—lament without agency.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R3-02
**Locus:** L2107
**Quote/anchor:** “Connections may be found with the units before (the general theme of injustice; cf. 3:16-22) and after (cf. 5:8-9 [English 5:9-10]).… the theme of oppression is significantly different, focusing on the absence of any consolation or hope for the oppressed”
**Claim:** Longman links 4:1–3 to injustice (3:16–22) and later 5:8–9 ET 5:9–10, but treats this unit as distinct for its stress on no consolation/hope for the oppressed.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R3-03
**Locus:** L2109
**Quote/anchor:** “such a perspective on the topic of oppression seems awkward when attributed to the mind of Solomon.… he, according to the historical books, contributed heavily to it in the last days of his life (1 Kings 11). This passage is a subtle signal… that the relationship between Solomon and Qohelet… is a literary and rhetorical one.”
**Claim:** Longman: 4:1–3’s passive view of oppression is awkward if Solomon is the speaker (Solomon could have acted; 1 Kgs 11 depicts him as contributing to oppression)—evidence that Solomonic framing is literary/rhetorical, not historical authorship.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R3-04
**Locus:** L2111–L2117; 4:1
**Quote/anchor:** “I observed… oh, the tears of the oppressed… he does not personally engage the subject or enjoin others to resist… He simply resigns himself… Michael Fox points out that this is true of all the passages in which he treats oppression (3:16; 8:9, 10): ‘He is just sorry that we must see these things.’”
**Claim:** Longman (citing Fox): Qohelet observes oppression clinically, is briefly overwhelmed (“oh, the tears”), but neither resists nor calls others to act—he is sorry we must see it (cf. 3:16; 8:9–10).

### C-R3-05
**Locus:** L2119–L2123; 4:1–2
**Quote/anchor:** “Note the twofold repetition of… There is no one to comfort them.… recognized as a stylistic trait of Qohelet (see 3:16).… It is better off to be dead than to live in such a world.… first of a number of so-called better-than proverbs.”
**Claim:** Double “no one to comfort them” is deliberate stylistic passion/despair (not to be emended). 4:2 is the first “better-than” proverb: death preferred to life under pervasive oppression; the dead no longer witness it.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R3-09
**Locus:** L2145–L2167; 4:4
**Quote/anchor:** “all toil and all success in work results from jealousy of ones neighbors. This too is meaningless and chasing the wind.… Graham Ogden… ‘rivalry’… James Crenshaw… Baba Batra 21a… turn Qohelet into an advocate of capitalism.… attempts to turn this negative observation into a positive one are ill-founded.… most jealousy or rivalry of neighbors is due to covetousness… tenth commandment”
**Claim:** Longman rejects positive/capitalist readings of *qin’ah* (Ogden “rivalry”; Crenshaw/B. Bat. 21a): jealousy here is selfish covetousness (Exod 20:17 / Deut 5:21), a never-satisfied motive → ceaseless work, *hebel* and chasing wind.

### C-R3-10
**Locus:** L2171–L2177; 4:5–6

**Claim:** 4:5 = proverb mocking lazy fools (not Ginsburg’s advocacy). 4:6 = better-than proverb for rest over toil; tension with 4:5 resolved by situational proverb logic—Qohelet prefers modest restful portion to jealous strife-toil; “chasing wind” stamps the proverb as his.

**Quote/anchor:** “Better the sight of the eyes than wandering desire. This is also meaningless and chasing the wind.… prefer… present… than what one only desires… ‘A bird in hand…’… final occurrence of the full form [hebel formula].… Desire cannot be fulfilled, and certainly the desire or even the attainment of wealth cannot provide satisfaction - it is all meaningless.”
**Claim:** Closing better-than proverb: present “sight of eyes” > roving *nephesh* (desire, not Whitley/Whybray “departing life”). Fits Qohelet’s here-and-now emphasis. Full *hebel* + chasing wind formula’s last occurrence; seals wealth/desire unit as meaningless.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R3-44
**Locus:** L2557–L2561; SUMMARY OF 4:17–6:9
**Quote/anchor:** “relate to the deity… caution. God is not a being whom one should bother or cross.… fulfill your obligation.… meaninglessness of wealth.… enjoyment is rare.… Only… God gives not only wealth but also the ability to enjoy it… buffered from the harsh pain of real life. In actuality, wealth too is meaningless.”
**Claim:** Longman unit summary: (1) cult = caution—don’t bother/cross God; keep vows if made; (2) wealth *hebel*—enjoyment rare, only when God dual-gifts wealth + capacity to enjoy as buffer; otherwise wealth meaningless.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]
